headline: Supply and demand: the price is just where the two lines cross

body: Demand slopes down (cheaper → people want more); supply slopes up (pricier → sellers offer more). The market price isn't set by either side alone — it's the single point where the quantity people want to buy equals the quantity sellers want to sell.
more:
The useful part is what happens when something shifts a whole line. A frost that wipes out a coffee crop slides the supply line left: at every price there's less coffee, so the crossing point moves up and to the left — higher price, less sold. A viral health study that makes everyone want avocados slides demand right: higher price, more sold.

This is why "the price went up" never tells you the cause on its own. Price rising with volume rising means demand grew; price rising with volume falling means supply shrank. The two diagnoses call for opposite responses.

body: A US dollar from 1913 — the year the Federal Reserve was founded and the modern price index begins — buys roughly what 31 dollars do today. Put the other way round, the dollar has shed about 97% of its purchasing power in a century.
more:
This isn't the result of dramatic crashes; it's the quiet compounding of low inflation. Average a bit over 3% a year and prices roughly double every two decades — five doublings in a century is a 32-fold rise.

It's also why "keeping it safe" under the mattress is not actually safe: cash held still loses purchasing power every single year. The number is an argument for owning assets that at least keep pace with prices, not against money itself.

headline: People will forget what you said, and forget what you did, but people will never forget how you made them feel.
body: It lands because memory is selective in exactly this way: we encode the emotional gist of an interaction far more durably than its content. A month later the facts of a meeting blur, but the feeling of being respected — or dismissed — stays sharp, and quietly drives how we treat that person next time.

headline: The unexamined life is not worth living.
body: Socrates said it facing a death sentence, having been offered exile if he'd just stop questioning everything. He refused: a life lived on unexamined autopilot — inherited opinions never tested, choices never questioned — wasn't, to him, a fully human life at all. The line is a challenge, not a comfort: it asks whether your beliefs are actually yours, or just the ones you happened to absorb.
